catalog_quote: Règle 1 L'accent d'intensité frappe la syllabe initiale des mots pleins. Les monosyllabes lexèmes le reçoivent également. Il n'est pas noté dans cette position au cours du présent travail: 'kai « manger des féculents » 'pirixa 'piriya « espiègle » 'néxùrù ... « champ d'ignames » (synthème analysable en deux segments, mais fonctionnant ... comme un élément simple) 'aa « ramer » o « fils » ... Il peut également se réaliser sur des mots-outils, les pronoms par exemple: 'gè-rré 'ge-rre « nous » 'cu-ru « eux deux » noté gèrré noté curu Règle 2 3.2. L'accent met en relief dans la chaîne les monosyllabes lexicaux et les éléments radicaux pleins. [p. 125] ... 3.3. Cependant, l'accent n'est pas sur l'initiale dans certains cas: a) L'accent peut être réalisé sur la seconde syllabe ou la seconde more des syllabes longues: va'rui « lune » (') aayo'ö (') aayɔɔ « limace (terme générique) » (le signe (') indique un accent secondaire; cf. 3.19.) (') daa'au? « abasourdi; réverbération de la lumière » ka'a « chose » En synchronie, il est impossible de donner les raisons de cette place accentuelle: les lexèmes de ce type sont donc appris comme tels par les locuteurs. b) Par contre, l'accent se « justifie » par l'application de la règle 1 dans les innombrables composés. [p. 126] ... si ces éléments ne sont pas monosyllabiques, l'accent signale à l'auditeur le radical ou le début du monème [p. 133]

sweep_summary: Ajië (ajie1238) is not in the catalog. The single target item, Kasarhérou/de la Fontinelle 1961 'Prosodèmes de la langue mélanésienne de Houaïlou' (BSL 56(1): 181–201), is a first-hand prosodic description of this language (relevance confirmed by Haudricourt's 1977 BSL review of the 1976 book, which names it as the first signalling of Houaïlou's 'type prosodique très particulier'), but no open copy exists: archive.org's BSL run skips 1939–1969, Gallica has no 1961 BSL, HathiTrust is search-only and could not be reached by automated download. Priority high. Screening the 17 open BSL volumes (1970–1979) on archive.org yielded two second-hand characterizations: Haudricourt 1974 (BSL 69(2): 315–316) — Houaïlou has 'ton glottal', not pitch tone, the marked glottalized prosodeme corresponding to marked high tone in Paicî/Cèmuhî and marked low tone in the far south — and Haudricourt 1977 (BSL 72(2), review 171) — the 1976 book's phonology (pp. 17–148) gives the full description by generation and dialect. Rivierre 1978 (BSL 73(1)) describes initial accent in Xârâcùù and is silent on Ajië. None states stress placement for Ajië, so no new stress statement was found. Best acquisition targets: de la Fontinelle 1976 (Harvard print, (a scan can be requested through your own library); HathiTrust mdp.39015024001482 search-only) and the 1961 article (BSL 56, print); secondary: Tryon et al. 1995 A'jië sketch (DOI 10.1515/9783110884012.2.859, paywalled) and de la Fontinelle 1979. new_statements.translation: Rule 1: The intensity accent strikes the initial syllable of full words. Lexical monosyllables receive it too. It is not marked in this position in the present work: 'kai 'eat starchy food' [p. 125] … 3.3. However, the accent is not on the initial syllable in certain cases: a) The accent may be realized on the second syllable, or the second mora of long syllables: va'rui 'moon' […] Synchronically it is impossible to give the reasons for this accent placement: lexemes of this type are therefore learned as such by speakers. b) By contrast, the accent is 'justified' by the application of Rule 1 in the innumerable compounds. [p. 126]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level intensity stress (accent d'intensité) falls on the first syllable of every full word (lexical word/radical), including lexical monosyllables; function words (mots-outils such as pronouns) are unstressed; in compounds the stress marks the radical, i.e. the beginning of the lexical element (p. 133: 'l'accent signale à l'auditeur le radical ou le début du monème'). A limited set of lexemes carry stress on the second syllable or second mora instead, unpredictably. Superimposed on this is a lexically placed 'accent glottalisé' (a glottal tone/accent, realized as an intensity accent with abrupt glottal closure) which may follow but never precede the intensity accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Discussed: two intensity accents cannot occupy contiguous syllables (p. 141); in words carrying a final glottalized accent, 'l'accent secondaire est l'accent démarcatif initial, l'accent primaire celui de la dernière more' (p. 132, e.g. 'aayo'o 'slug'); 'accent secondaire; cf. 3.19' mentioned for lexemes like daa'au (p. 126); accent-inducing suffixes (Règle 3, p. 127) can shift or add an accent, e.g. when the final syllable of the word is unaccented 'c'est l'antépénultième qui porte l'accent d'intensité' (p. 128).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexemes with accent on the second syllable/second mora (va'rui 'lune', daa'au 'abasourdi', ka'a 'chose'), learned as such; accent-inducing suffixes and suffix-driven shifts (§3.1x, pp. 127–128); function words unaccented; the older description by Leenhardt (1946, repeated in the 1961 BSL article) claimed instead a 'light tonic accent on the last syllable of the full word', which de la Fontinelle's description supersedes (the final prominence probably corresponds to her glottal accent / utterance-final demarcative accent).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme level: the rule is stated for 'mots pleins' (lexical words) and radicals within compounds, with a demarcative function; at utterance level an additional end-of-utterance demarcative accent falls on the last or penultimate syllable of the utterance (p. 144), and the intensity accent 'met en relief dans la chaîne les monosyllabes lexicaux et les éléments radicaux pleins' (Règle 2, p. 125). The author distinguishes this intensity accent from the 'accent glottalisé'/'ton glottal' (pp. 140–145), which Haudricourt (1974) treats as a glottal tone; Ajië is thus a stress language with a lexical glottal accent, not a musical-tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: de la Fontinelle 1976 describes 'la langue de Houaïlou' = A'jië (ajie1238), based on speakers from the Houaïlou region (a coastal 'bord de mer' consultant and older speakers; Haudricourt notes the description covers generations and dialects); Leenhardt's 'houaïlou' is the same language. No separate glottocode involved.

new_statements.quote: § 2. — Accent et ton. La langue est susurrante et fortement nasalisée. Dans les termes dissyllabiques ou monosyllabiques il y a un accent tonique léger sur la dernière syllabe du mot plein. Dans les composés, le mot plein garde l'accent, qu'il soit en position initiale ou finale. peva = père. pèvipo = discours de deuil, de po = lier. nagewe = tourner, de na = mettre. koroso = marée de sizygie, de ko = marée. Mais il arrive, dans certains mots de trois syllabes ayant trois voyelles similaires, que le mot se prononce sans accent aucun : kororo = déchet de pierre. Le mot plein final est toujours bref. Deux syllabes ayant la même consonne et la même voyelle peuvent se distinguer par une différence de hauteur musicale.
new_statements.translation: § 2. Accent and tone. The language is whispered and strongly nasalised. In disyllabic or monosyllabic terms there is a light tonic accent on the last syllable of the full word. In compounds, the full word keeps the accent, whether it stands in initial or final position. peva = father. pèvipo = mourning speech, from po = to bind. nagewe = to turn, from na = to put. koroso = spring tide, from ko = tide. But it happens, in certain three-syllable words having three similar vowels, that the word is pronounced with no accent at all: kororo = stone waste. The final full word is always short. Two syllables having the same consonant and the same vowel can be distinguished by a difference of musical pitch.

Same language and region (Leenhardt's 'AJIE, région Houaïlou: Monéo, Houaïlou, Kouaoua, Poya, Bourail, 4.000 indigènes'). The two are not reconciled by domain: both speak of the word. A plausible bridge is de La Fontinelle's own utterance-level rule (p. 133: at every pause the intensity accent strikes the last or penultimate syllable), which would make citation-form words sound final-accented to a pre-phonological observer; Leenhardt's pitch remarks anticipate what la…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A light 'accent tonique' falls on the last syllable of the full (lexical) word in monosyllables and disyllables; in compounds the lexical member keeps its accent whether it is initial or final in the compound. Leenhardt adds that words are further distinguished by pitch ('hauteur musicale'; he notes up to four pitch levels, e.g. ko¹ 'spirit' / ko² 'cloud' / ko³ 'be ashamed'), that the phrase has a rising melodic profile with the highest pitch on a phrase-final full word, and that a study of this 'ton musical' remains to be done.
new_statements.exceptions: Some trisyllabic words with three similar vowels are pronounced with no accent at all (kororo 'stone waste'); the accented full word in final position is always short; pitch (tone) distinctions between otherwise identical syllables, and a phrase-level melodic contour rising to the end.
new_statements.identity_note: Leenhardt 1946 describes 'AJIE, région Houaïlou' (aire: Monéo, Houaïlou, Kouaoua, Poya, Bourail; c. 4,000 speakers) — the same Houaïlou variety that de La Fontinelle 1976 (and Kasarhérou 1961) describe; no dialect split is at issue.

Cependant , un certain nombre de dissyllabes ayant deux voyelles brèves de même timbre et de même ton ont un accent également réparti sur les deux voyelles ; nous l'indiquons par le signe + . new_statements.translation: … the place of the accent has distinctive value; example: ɓi'ru 'to enter', 'ɓiru 'to sew'. However, a number of disyllables with two short vowels of the same quality and the same tone have an accent evenly spread over both vowels; we mark it with the sign +. Pitch modulations seem mostly to be determined by the place of the prosodic features listed above, the accent often being accompanied, as in English, by an abrupt melodic fall. Word accent can be modified by phrase accent. … [p. 181:] For a long time one wondered whether this was a [tone] language … In fact, the prosodic features of this language consist of glottalization and nasalization. new_statements.rule_in_words: In the visible text the author states that the PLACE of the word accent is distinctive (contrastive), with the minimal pair ɓi'ru 'enter' (accent on the 2nd syllable) vs 'ɓiru 'sew' (accent on the 1st); some disyllables with two identical short vowels of the same tone carry level accent on both vowels (marked +); the accent is often accompanied by an abrupt pitch fall, pitch being otherwise determined by the position of the prosodic features (glottalization, nasalization, accent); word accent can be overridden by phrase accent. The article's thesis (p. 181) is that Houaïlou is not a tone language: its prosodemes are glottalization and nasalization. No statement of a default (e.g. initial) accent position is visible in the snippets; the probes for 'syllabe initiale', 'première syllabe', 'accent d'intensité', 'frappe' returned nothing from this volume, so whether the full page also gives a default position remains unread.

new_statements.quote: 3.4 INITIAL STRESS. A small number of Oceanic languages have word-initial stress. This occurs in a number of Meso-Melanesian languages, like Tungag (Lesley Fast, pers. comm.), Tangga (Bell 1977), and Taiof (Ross TOL). Within Central-Eastern Oceanic, word-initial stress is common only in the languages of New Caledonia (Southern Oceanic linkage)—for example, Iaai (Ozanne-Rivierre 1976, Lynch TOL), Nyelâyu (Ozanne-Rivierre 1998), Xârâcùù (Moyse-Faurie 1995, Lynch TOL), Ajië (La Fontinelle 1976), and Tîrî (Osumi 1995)—and can probably be reconstructed for Proto-New Caledonian.
new_statements.citation: Lynch, John (2000). Reconstructing Proto-Oceanic Stress. Oceanic Linguistics 39(1): 53–82.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial stress = initial) and as the de La Fontinelle 1976 statement (Règle 1: accent on the initial syllable of full words). It is a secondary statement: Lynch's source for Ajië is La Fontinelle 1976 itself, so it adds no independent evidence, only a typological framing (initial stress as a Proto-New Caledonian feature, explained as reanalysed trochaic stress after right-edge erosion). It is at odds with Leenhardt 1946 (final accent), but Lynch does not cite or discuss Leenhardt.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lynch lists Ajië (citing La Fontinelle 1976) among the New Caledonian languages with word-initial stress, i.e. primary stress on the first syllable of the word; he treats initial stress as a shared New Caledonian feature reconstructible for Proto-New Caledonian. No Ajië examples are given; the only illustrative data in §3.4 are Nyelâyu.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Ajië or any New Caledonian language (the only secondary-stress remark in the paper is Ross's Proto-Oceanic view quoted in the abstract: 'secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the penultimate').
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ajië. §6.3 (p. 78) gives a diachronic account only: 'Word-initial stress is a feature of New Caledonian languages.. In most New Caledonian languages, there has been considerable erosion from the right, with the result that the majority of roots consist of only one or two syllables. If stress was assigned on the basis of syllabic trochees, primary stress would thus be on the initial syllable in nearly all words. It is quite possible that this was reinterpreted as initial- rather than penultimate-syllable stress, and generalized to the few roots that have more than two syllables.'
new_statements.identity_note: Lynch 2000 names the language 'Ajië' with La Fontinelle 1976 as source, i.e. the Houaïlou variety described in that book; no other dialect is named. Leenhardt 1946 likewise heads its section '1. AJIE région Houaïlou'. All three sources concern the same Houaïlou-region variety.

readall_conflicts: Leenhardt 1946 (p. 13, § 2 'Accent et ton') states a light tonic accent on the last syllable of the full word (final), whereas the catalog record and the existing statement from de La Fontinelle 1976 (p. 125, Règle 1) state that the accent d'intensité strikes the initial syllable of full words, with exceptions on the second syllable/more of long syllables (p. 126) and a demarcative utterance-final accent on the last or penultimate syllable before any pause (p. 133). The two sources describe the same variety (Houaïlou). The 1976 monograph is the dedicated phonological description by the author who also wrote the 1961 'Prosodèmes' article, while Leenhardt's 1946 paragraph is a brief impressionistic note in a 36-language survey that itself calls for a proper study of the language's pitch; its final-accent observation is most naturally read as the utterance-final demarcative prominence de La Fontinelle describes. The catalog's initial reading therefore stands, but the Leenhardt statement should be recorded as a dissenting older source; Kasarhérou 1961, which could not be opened, is the work that would settle. One disagreement stands among the sources, and Lynch 2000 does not resolve it independently. De La Fontinelle 1976 (Règle 1, p. 125) puts the intensity accent on the initial syllable of full words, with exceptions on the second syllable or second mora of long syllables (§3.3, p. 126) and a separate utterance-level demarcative accent on the last or penultimate syllable befor…

sources.quote: 3.4 INITIAL STRESS. A small number of Oceanic languages have word-initial stress. This occurs in a number of Meso-Melanesian languages, like Tungag (Lesley Fast, pers. comm.), Tangga (Bell 1977), and Taiof (Ross TOL). Within Central-Eastern Oceanic, word-initial stress is common only in the languages of New Caledonia (Southern Oceanic linkage)—for example, Iaai (Ozanne-Rivierre 1976, Lynch TOL), Nyelâyu (Ozanne-Rivierre 1998), Xârâcùù (Moyse-Faurie 1995, Lynch TOL), Ajië (La Fontinelle 1976), and Tîrî (Osumi 1995)—and can probably be reconstructed for Proto-New Caledonian.
sources.locator: p. 63, §3.4 'Initial stress' (PDF page 11 of 30; the scanned text); also p. 78, §6.3 'Development of initial stress' (PDF page 26; the scanned text)
sources.note: Comparative survey of Oceanic stress that may summarize New Caledonian (incl. Ajië) stress from de la Fontinelle/Rivierre; unverified.

sources.quote: … la place de l'accent a valeur distinctive ; exemple : ẞi'ru , entrer , 'ẞiru , coudre . Cependant , un certain nombre de dissyllabes ayant deux voyelles brèves de même timbre et de même ton ont un accent également réparti sur les deux voyelles ; nous l'indiquons par le signe + . Les modulations de hauteur semblent surtout être déterminées par la place des traits prosodiques ci-dessus énumérés , l'accent s'accompagnant souvent , comme en anglais , d'une brusque descente mélodique . L'accent de mot peut être modifié par l'accent de phrase . … [p. 181 opening:] … On s'est demandé pendant longtemps s'il s'agissait d'une langue … tons . En fait , les traits prosodiques de cette langue consistent en glottalisation et nasalisation . …

sources.quote: § 2. — Accent et ton. La langue est susurrante et fortement nasalisée. Dans les termes dissyllabiques ou monosyllabiques il y a un accent tonique léger sur la dernière syllabe du mot plein. Dans les composés, le mot plein garde l'accent, qu'il soit en position initiale ou finale. peva = père. pèvipo = discours de deuil, de po = lier. nagewe = tourner, de na = mettre. koroso = marée de sizygie, de ko = marée. Mais il arrive, dans certains mots de trois syllabes ayant trois voyelles similaires, que le mot se prononce sans accent aucun : kororo = déchet de pierre. Le mot plein final est toujours bref. Deux syllabes ayant la même consonne et la même voyelle peuvent se distinguer par une différence de hauteur musicale.
sources.locator: p. 13 (Gallica view f60), Première partie, III. Langues du groupe du Sud, 1. AJIE région Houaïlou, § 2 'Accent et ton'; cf. p. 11 (view f58), end of chapter II Phonétique: 'Il reste à connaître l'accent, le ton, et les particularités phonétiques de chaque langue. On en trouvera le détail au chapitre réservé à chacune de celles-ci.'
sources.note: Contains the competing older claim 'accent tonique léger sur la dernière syllabe du mot plein' for Houaïlou; the Gallica scan is open but its text/ALTO/PDF endpoints served a security challenge by automated download.

sources.citation: Haudricourt, André-Georges (1974). Compte rendu no. 177 of J.-C. Rivierre, Phonologie comparée des dialectes de l'extrême-sud de la Nouvelle-Calédonie (SELAF 1973). Bulletin de la Société de Linguistique de Paris 69(2): 315–316.
sources.quote: Or, dans la région intermédiaire, nous avons la langue Houailou, dont Mme de La Fontinelle vient de donner une description dans une thèse à l'impression, langue qui n'est pas à ton musical mais à ton glottal ; et il me semble bien que c'est ce ton glottal « marqué » qui correspond au ton marqué des langues à ton musical ; ainsi un arbre usuel le « gayac » Acacia spirorbis Lab. a un ton haut dans les langues du centre, glottalisé en Houailou, et bas à l'extrême-sud. [Translation: In the intermediate region we have the Houaïlou language, which Mme de la Fontinelle has just described in a thesis in press, a language that has not a musical (pitch) tone but a glottal tone; and it seems to me that this marked glottal tone corresponds to the marked tone of the pitch-tone languages; thus a common tree, the gaiac, has a high tone in the central languages, is glottalized in Houaïlou, and has low tone in the far south.]
sources.locator: BSL 69(2) 1974, comptes rendus, no. 177, pp. 315–316 (the scanned textof the copy consulted)
sources.note: Second-hand (reporting de la Fontinelle's then-unprinted thesis) but the only explicit statement of Ajië's prosodic type read in this search of works with stress in the title: Houaïlou is not a pitch-tone language but has a 'glottal tone' — a marked glottalized prosodeme that corresponds to the marked high tone of the central languages (Paicî/Cèmuhî) and the marked low tone of the far south. No statement of where word stress falls.
